subject: Immunology
vignette: A 28-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a serum antibody that binds a nuclear antigen but does not fix complement when tested in vitro. Investigators isolate the antibody and digest it with papain, which cleaves the molecule into three fragments. Two fragments each retain antigen binding but cannot precipitate antigen or bind complement. The third fragment crystallizes and supports complement fixation.
question: The antigen-binding specificity of the two papain-generated fragments is conferred by which of the following structures?

options.text: The Fc region, because it determines the isotype and effector function
The J chain, which links monomeric units into multimers
Paired variable domains (VH + VL) at the amino termini of the Fab arms
Constant domains of the heavy chain (CH2 and CH3)
The switch region DNA upstream of the constant genes

explanation_correct: Papain cleaves immunoglobulin just proximal to the inter-heavy-chain disulfide bonds, yielding two identical Fab fragments and one Fc fragment. Each Fab contains one complete light chain (VL + CL) and the VH + CH1 portion of a heavy chain, and the antigen-combining site is formed by the hypervariable loops of the paired VH and VL domains. Because the variable regions differ between antibody molecules, they carry the antigen specificity, whereas the papain-resistant Fc fragment carries the effector functions of complement fixation, Fc receptor binding, and placental transfer.

explanation_incorrect.A: The Fc fragment contains the constant CH2 and CH3 domains and mediates effector functions, but it lacks the variable loops that generate antigen specificity.
explanation_incorrect.B: The J chain is a small polypeptide that joins monomeric immunoglobulins into polymers such as dimeric IgA and pentameric IgM; it plays no part in antigen recognition.
explanation_incorrect.D: The CH2 and CH3 constant domains are part of the Fc and do not vary between antibodies against different antigens, so they cannot determine specificity.
explanation_incorrect.E: Switch regions are DNA sequences upstream of constant-region genes that enable class switching; they change isotype, not antigen-binding specificity.

educationalObjective: Papain splits immunoglobulin into two Fab arms (paired VH + VL, the antigen-binding sites) and one Fc fragment (constant effector domains).

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 3-year-old boy with recurrent sinopulmonary infections undergoes serum immunofixation. Circulating antibodies are detectable, but several of them are functionally defective in complement activation and phagocyte binding. The laboratory technologist explains that the antibody class of each molecule is identified on the test because all molecules of one class share a particular region.
question: Differences in the heavy-chain constant regions of immunoglobulins are responsible for which of the following?

options.text: Antigen-binding affinity for a hapten
The hypervariable complementarity-determining regions
Junctional diversity generated by RAG recombination
The isotype (class) and its associated effector functions
Somatic hypermutation in germinal centers

explanation_correct: On the basis of the constant region of the heavy chain, immunoglobulins are divided into the five isotypes: IgM (mu), IgD (delta), IgG (gamma), IgA (alpha), and IgE (epsilon). The heavy-chain constant region defines the class and therefore dictates which effector functions an antibody can perform, such as complement activation, binding to Fc receptors on phagocytes, placental transfer by IgG, or mast cell sensitization by IgE. All antibodies of the same isotype share this constant region, which is why the class can be detected antigenically.

explanation_incorrect.A: Affinity for antigen is determined by the variable (VH + VL) regions; the constant region has no role in hapten binding.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hypervariable complementarity-determining regions are located within the variable domains of both heavy and light chains, not in constant domains.
explanation_incorrect.C: Junctional diversity arises from RAG-mediated recombination of V, D, and J gene segments in the variable region, not from the constant region.
explanation_incorrect.E: Somatic hypermutation targets the variable region genes to increase affinity; the constant region is unaffected.

educationalObjective: The heavy-chain constant region defines the isotype (IgM, IgD, IgG, IgA, IgE) and its effector functions, while variable regions determine antigen specificity.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 6-year-old girl has a severe reaction to a blood transfusion and is found to have antibodies directed against ABO blood group antigens. Her immunologist explains that the antibody binding site is a small pocket of about 10-12 amino acids made of heavy- and light-chain peptides folded together at the tip of the Fab arm.
question: These hypervariable regions form which part of the antibody molecule?

options.text: The complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) of the variable domains
The CH3 domains of the Fc fragment
The hinge region disulfide bonds
The transmembrane portion of the heavy chain
The leader signal peptide sequence

explanation_correct: Each Fab arm ends in two variable domains, VH on the heavy chain and VL on the light chain. Within these variable domains, three hypervariable loops, the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs), form the actual antigen-binding site. The enormous diversity of CDR sequences, generated by recombination, junctional diversity, and somatic hypermutation, allows an individual to make antibodies against virtually any antigen, including the carbohydrate ABO antigens that provoked this transfusion reaction.

explanation_incorrect.B: CH3 domains are constant regions at the far end of the Fc and mediate interactions with Fc receptors, not antigen binding.
explanation_incorrect.C: The hinge region provides flexibility between the Fab arms and the Fc but does not contact antigen directly.
explanation_incorrect.D: The transmembrane portion anchors membrane-bound immunoglobulin on B cells and is irrelevant to the antigen-binding pocket.
explanation_incorrect.E: The leader signal peptide directs the nascent chain into the endoplasmic reticulum and is cleaved off during secretion.

educationalObjective: The antigen-binding site of an antibody is formed by the hypervariable CDR loops of the paired VH and VL domains at the tip of each Fab arm.

subject: Immunology
vignette: A 42-year-old woman is treated with infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal antibody, for Crohn disease. Six weeks later she develops joint pains, fever, and a serum sickness-like reaction. Testing shows anti-drug antibodies. Her physician explains that the constant portion of infliximab is human but that the antigen-binding portion is derived from mouse protein. A second patient receiving a fully humanized antibody does not develop anti-drug antibodies.
question: In a chimeric antibody like infliximab, which portion is most likely to be recognized as foreign and elicit the anti-drug antibody response?

options.text: The human Fc region
The mouse-derived variable (Fab) regions
The glycosylphosphatidylinositol anchor
The secretory component added during transcytosis
The J chain linking monomers into polymers

explanation_correct: Chimeric antibodies such as infliximab have mouse variable regions, the Fab antigen-binding portion, fused to human constant regions. Because the variable region sequence is of mouse origin and differs from any self human sequence, the patient's immune system can mount an anti-drug antibody response, which may neutralize the drug and cause infusion or serum sickness-like reactions. Humanized and fully human antibodies reduce, though do not always eliminate, this immunogenicity.

explanation_incorrect.A: The Fc of a chimeric antibody is human and therefore generally non-immunogenic; it is the same sequence found in native human IgG.
explanation_incorrect.C: Immunoglobulins are secreted glycoproteins and are not anchored by a GPI anchor, so this does not contribute to immunogenicity here.
explanation_incorrect.D: The secretory component belongs to polymeric IgA produced at mucosa and has no relevance to a systemically administered monoclonal IgG.
explanation_incorrect.E: J chains are present only in polymeric IgA and IgM, not in a monomeric therapeutic IgG monoclonal antibody.

educationalObjective: Chimeric therapeutic antibodies pair mouse variable (Fab) regions with human constant regions, and the mouse-derived variable region is the main immunogenic target.
